scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Finger tutting evolved from 'tutting,' a street dance style inspired by the 2D poses of ancient Egyptian art.
Its modern iteration as a finger-specific discipline gained significant momentum around 2010.
Key figures like Jay 'Jsmooth' Gutierrez and Julian 'JayFunk' Daniels are credited with innovating and popularizing the style through film credits and viral commercials.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a form of self-expression within street dance culture, finger tutting has become a staple of digital performance art.
It is used in competitive dance battles, commercial advertising, and as a cinematic shorthand for magic or technical interface manipulation.
It represents a fusion of physical skill and geometric logic.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by articulating the fingers and thumbs to create geometric shapes, primarily squares and rectangles.
It relies on 90-degree angles and the isolation of finger joints.
Practitioners often use their palms as a base or 'floor' for the fingers to move across.
Watch for The King Tut Box, Digital Waves.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Finger tutting is typically performed to hip-hop, electronic, or 'glitch' music that features sharp, percussive beats.
The movements are often synchronized with 'clicks,' 'pops,' or 'snaps' in the audio track.
Listen for the Synthesizers, Drum machines, Electronic percussion.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 100 beats a minute.

The music is characterized by crisp, clean electronic beats that provide clear 'points' for the dancer to hit. It often features a heavy emphasis on the snare or 'click' sounds to mirror the snapping movements of the finger joints.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: There is no specific traditional costume, though practitioners often wear clothing that does not obstruct the view of the hands.
In some contexts, such as 'gloving,' dancers may wear LED-lit gloves to enhance the visual effect of the movements.
The setting is often urban or digital, frequently filmed in close-up to capture the small-scale detail of the fingers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key practitioners include Jay 'Jsmooth' Gutierrez, who showcased the style in Step Up 3D; Julian 'JayFunk' Daniels, known for the 'Unleash Your Fingers' campaign; and John 'Pnut' Hunt, whose 'Greasy Fingers' video and appearance in Taylor Swift's 'Shake It Off' brought the style to a mass audience.

While it is a global digital phenomenon, variants exist in how it is integrated into other styles, such as its use in K-pop choreography (e.g., Red Velvet) or its intersection with the 'gloving' community in the electronic dance music (EDM) scene.
Finger tutting is a direct descendant of 'tutting' (King Tut), which itself is a branch of the 'popping' and 'funk styles' family of street dance.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Finger Tutting is parent of Tutting: Finger tutting is a specialized micro-version of the original arm-based tutting style.
Finger Tutting is sibling of Gloving: Both styles focus on intricate hand movements, often sharing the same geometric patterns.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: The Box: Create a square shape using the index fingers and thumbs of both hands.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid rounded or soft angles; the style requires 'hard' 90-degree corners to maintain the illusion.
Teachers of this dance warn against: trying to do finger tutting with tense or stiff hands
